gx.meta.title: Digital Galaxy · {brand}
gx.meta.desc: Shape a galaxy of light in your browser: spiral, barred spiral, elliptical and irregular, the families astronomers use to describe galaxies. An interactive world of {brand}.
gx.lead: The four families of galaxies, rebuilt from points of light. Choose a shape, stir the stars with your pointer and fly into the core.
gx.d.spiral: A flat, rotating disc with arms of young blue stars winding out from a bright central bulge. Example: the Andromeda Galaxy.
gx.d.barred: A straight bar of stars crosses the centre and the spiral arms begin at its ends. Our own Milky Way is a barred spiral.
gx.d.elliptical: A smooth, featureless ellipsoid of mostly older, redder stars, with little gas left to form new ones. Example: Messier 87.
gx.d.irregular: No orderly shape, often pulled out of form by the gravity of neighbouring galaxies. Example: the Large Magellanic Cloud.
gx.hint: Drag to orbit · Scroll or pinch to zoom · Move the pointer to stir the stars
gx.hint.kb: Keyboard: focus the galaxy, then arrow keys orbit and + / − zoom
gx.nogl: Your browser could not start 3D graphics (WebGL), so you are seeing a photograph of a real nebula instead. Everything else on this page still works.
gx.err: The 3D scene stopped unexpectedly. Reload the page to try again.
gx.note: A procedural simulation for exploring shapes, not a scientific model. Not to scale.
gx.fact: Light from the Andromeda Galaxy takes about 2.5 million years to reach Earth.
gx.about.p1: In the 1920s and 1930s the astronomer Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies by their shape: ellipticals, spirals and barred spirals, with irregular galaxies as the ones that fit no family. His “tuning fork” diagram, published in 1936, is still the usual starting point for describing galaxies.
gx.about.p2: Every point here is placed by a few simple rules: how far it sits from the centre, which arm it follows and how warm its colour is. Inner stars complete their orbits sooner, so the arms slowly wind up as you watch. Real spiral arms do not wind up like this; astronomers call that puzzle the winding problem and explain the arms as density waves.
gx.about.p3: Built with Three.js and a custom GLSL shader. The number of stars adapts to your device, and the animation pauses when you leave the tab or prefer reduced motion.

wd.1: Real 3D clothes, shoes, bags, watches and jewellery. Turn them, pick a part and change its colour.
wh.1: Pick a tab at the top. Drag to turn the model, then choose a part and a colour.
wd.2: A capsule wardrobe planner. Build a small rack of clothes and see every outfit it makes, which ones are colour-harmonious, and a week of looks that rotates pieces evenly.
wh.2: Tap a piece to recolour or remove it. Add pieces from the panel. Everything is saved in this browser.
wd.3: A sneaker configurator for an original Abidora shoe. Pick any part, give it a colour and a material, save your colourways and export them.
wh.3: Click any part of the shoe, then a swatch. Try a starting point or a random colourway.
wd.4: A watch atelier. Compose your own watch and it keeps real time, with today’s date, the real moon phase, a second time zone on a GMT hand, a working chronograph and a turning dive bezel.
wh.4: Change case, dial, markers and hands. Start the chronograph. Scroll over the watch to turn the dive bezel.
wd.5: A gem light lab. A faceted stone sparkles as you move the light, and a ray tracer through its profile shows with Snell’s law and total internal reflection why cut proportions decide how much light comes back.
wh.5: Move the pointer over the gem. Change the pavilion angle and watch the rays in the profile: yellow comes back to the eye, red leaks out.
wd.6: A tote bag pattern maker. Enter the size you want and get the cut list, a layout on your fabric width, how much fabric to buy, sewing steps and a full-size printable pattern.
wh.6: Set the finished size and options. Print the SVG pattern at 100% scale and check the 10 cm square before cutting.
wd.7: A streetwear graphic maker in the screen-print tradition: stacked outlines, arcs, waves and repeats, two-ink misregistration and halftone, previewed on a tee and exported for print.
wh.7: Type your words, pick a layout and a colour story. Export a transparent 3000 px print file. Print only words you have the right to use.
wd.8: A palette lab built on colour theory. Generate colour stories by harmony and mood, or extract one from your own photo, then check text contrast and see it worn as an outfit.
wh.8: Press space for a new palette and lock the colours you like. Photos are analysed in your browser and never uploaded.
wd.9: Fabric physics: a cloth made of particles and springs, with silk, cotton, denim, wool and chiffon each moving, stretching and tearing in its own way.
wh.9: Drag the cloth, switch to scissors to cut it, pin it in new places, and turn up the wind.
wd.10: A century of silhouettes, 1900 to 1999. One parametric dress morphs through the decades, from the Edwardian S-bend to the 1990s slip, with a short note on each era.
wh.10: Scrub the year slider or play the century. Turn on the previous era to compare shapes.
wd.11: Abidora Circuit: a 3D race at sunset. Three laps of a 1.9 km track against three rivals, with real car physics for power, grip and drag, drifting that fills your nitro, and easy touch controls on phones. Every car is a real 3D model.
wh.11: Choose a car and a difficulty, then press Start race. Keyboard: arrows or W A S D to drive, Space to drift, Shift for nitro, C to change the camera. Phone: the game opens full screen; steer with ◀ ▶ on the left, the gas is automatic (or switch to manual), and Drift and Nitro are on the right.
wd.12: An electric road-trip planner. Set the car, distance, speed and outside temperature, and it plans charging stops, battery level along the route, total time and energy cost.
wh.12: Move the sliders for distance, speed and temperature. The timeline and battery chart redraw at once; the lower chart shows how speed changes range.
wd.13: A lean-angle lab. A motorcycle laps a circuit and the lean every corner needs is calculated from speed and radius, with tyre grip and ground clearance setting the limit.
wh.13: Choose a bike, a surface and how fast to ride. Green parts of the line need little lean, red parts are past the limit. The rear view shows the lean live.
wd.14: The history of the car as a printed archive. Fourteen milestones from 1886 to 2010 on a timeline you can filter by theme, plus a game: put the inventions in order.
wh.14: Click a dot, or tab to it and press Enter. In “Put it in order”, drag the cards or use the arrows, then check your score.
wd.15: A concept-car wind tunnel. Drag the points of a car’s profile and a real lattice-Boltzmann air-flow solver shows speed, pressure and swirl around it and measures the drag.
wh.15: Start from a preset, drag the white points to reshape the body, wait for the drag index to settle, then press Record drag to compare shapes.
wd.16: An aircraft explorer. Design a NACA wing section, set angle of attack, speed and altitude, and see the lift, stall speed and air density from the standard atmosphere.
wh.16: Change camber and thickness to shape the wing, pick an aircraft class, then raise the angle of attack until it stalls. Try the same speed high up.
wd.17: An orbit sandbox. A spacecraft circles Earth under real gravity; fire engine burns to reshape the orbit, and a Hohmann planner calculates and flies a transfer to a new altitude.
wh.17: Choose a burn size and press Prograde or Retrograde. Or set a target altitude and press Fly the transfer. Speed up time with the warp buttons.
wd.18: Commute compare. Enter your trip and see how walking, cycling, e-bikes, scooters, buses, rail and cars compare over a year in time, money, CO₂ and calories, with a race to see who arrives first.
wh.18: Set your distance and days a week. Sort by time, cost or CO₂. Open any mode to change its speed, fares and emission factor for your city.
wd.19: Architecture in real 3D. Walk into a travertine-and-glass pavilion under the real sun of eight cities, change the day and the hour, try classic proportions, and hang a brick arch from a true catenary.
wh.19: Drag to turn; scroll or pinch to zoom. Press “Walk inside” to walk with WASD or the thumb stick. In the panel pick a city, day and hour, or press “Play a day”. Proportion changes the bays; Arch sets the gate's span and rise.
wd.20: A room planner in 3D at true size. Place a sofa, bed, table and more; the planner flags collisions, a blocked door swing and walkways under 60 cm, while the sun moves through the window.
wh.20: Tap a piece and drag it across the floor; it snaps to 5 cm. Use “Turn 90°” and “Remove”, add pieces from the list, and change the room size, floor and walls. Switch between 3D view and Floor plan, and save a picture.
num.label: In numbers
cr.data: Star positions, star names and constellation lines in the Astronomy Observatory world come from d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD 3-Clause licence). Planet and Moon positions are calculated on your device. Coastlines in the World Explorer world come from Natural Earth 1:110m (public domain), via the world-atlas package (ISC licence).
wd.21: A 15-minute city at night in 3D. Paint homes, shops, offices, parks and transit on a 2.4 km grid; every home measures its walk to each, and the score, residents and green space update live.
wh.21: Choose what to paint and drag across the city. Use “Move camera” to turn and zoom, or start from a ready-made city. The View tab shows the walk-time heat map and a fly-over.
wd.22: An envelope and energy studio. Choose a climate, insulation, windows and airtightness, and see a home's yearly heating, cooling and rooftop solar, so you can chase a near-zero house.
wh.22: Change one setting at a time and watch where the heat goes and the yearly totals. The numbers use simplified, published rules of thumb, not a full building simulation.
wd.23: A bookcase studio. Design the shelves and a real beam formula shows how far each one will sag under books, today and years from now as wood creeps. Export the cut list.
wh.23: Set the size, bays, board and what goes on the shelves, and choose shelves resting on pins or fixed at both ends. Read the sag now and after a year, then download the cut list as CSV.
wd.24: A gear train studio. Real involute gears are drawn from their maths, mesh at the right distance and turn at the right speeds. Read the ratio, output speed and torque, and export a gear as SVG.
wh.24: Choose how many gears, select one to set its teeth, then set the module and input speed. Pause to study the mesh, and export the selected gear as SVG in millimetres.
wd.25: A packaging studio on a designer's desk. Enter a product's size, design the print, and watch the real dieline fold into a 3D box. Download the dieline in millimetres and the artwork for a printer.
wh.25: Set length, width and height and choose a print sheet. In Artwork, type a brand and tagline and pick colours and a pattern. Press “Fold it up” or use the Fold slider, then download the dieline (SVG) and the artwork (PNG).
wd.26: A keystone studio. Looking up at a building makes its walls lean inward; drag four corners onto something truly rectangular and a perspective transform straightens it, like a tilt-shift lens.
wh.26: Drag the four handles onto the corners of a window or facade, then press Straighten. Load your own photo; it never leaves your browser.
wd.27: Living type. A word set in huge letters becomes a window onto a generated landscape of ridges, forest, water and sky, and every layer moves at its own depth as you move.
wh.27: Type your own word, pick the letter that becomes an oval window, then choose the season, the hour and a new landscape. Move the pointer to look around, and save it as a wallpaper.
wd.28: Ocean World. A living sea built from real wave physics: sail the swell, then dive through sunlit water to a reef with a school of fish.
wh.28: Drag to look around and pinch or scroll to zoom. The buttons fly you to the surface, a dive, the reef floor or the buoy. In the panel, set the swell, wind, depth and sun; the gauges show pressure, temperature and which colours of light still reach you.
wd.29: Forest World. One hectare of woodland grows tree by tree: pioneers race for the light, shade-tolerant trees take over, and fire or storm starts the story again.
wh.29: Drag to look around, walk in among the trees or see the canopy from above. In the panel, pick a starting plot and the speed, then try a wildfire, a storm or thinning. Tap a tree to see its species, height, age and light.
wd.30: Wildlife Kingdom. A golden-hour meadow where every hare and fox lives, eats and breeds on its own, and the populations rise and fall in cycles beside the Lotka–Volterra equations.
wh.30: Drag to look around. Follow a fox, drop into the grass or watch from above. In the panel, change grass regrowth, hunting skill and speed, release animals or remove the foxes, and watch the live chart. Tap an animal to see its energy and age.
wd.31: Murmuration and song. A starling flock where each bird watches its seven nearest neighbours, as real starlings do, scattering from a falcon you steer; a second panel turns bird song into a live spectrogram.
wh.31: Move the pointer to steer the falcon, or press Scatter them. Tune personal space, heading matching and staying together. In the song panel, open a recording or use your microphone; nothing is uploaded.
wd.32: Mountain Explorer. Peaks carved by rain, a snow line and tree line set by how air cools with height, and real hiking times for the route you draw.
wh.32: Drag to orbit and pinch to zoom. Tap the ground to add waypoints; the panel shows distance, climb, walking time and the coldest point. Change the valley temperature to move the snow and tree lines, then fly the route.
wd.33: The colour of depth. Water swallows light one colour at a time; this world filters a real photo, or yours, with the Beer–Lambert law so you see what a diver sees at any depth, with a gauge for pressure, temperature and safe breathing gases.
wh.33: Drag the depth and the distance to the subject, then switch between daylight, strobe and colour-corrected. Choose clear ocean or green coast, use your own photo, and save the image.
wd.34: Aurora watch. Pick a place and a geomagnetic storm level, and the world works out where the auroral oval sits, how far away the lights are and how high they rise above your horizon, then paints the sky you would see.
wh.34: Choose a place, type your own coordinates or use your location (it stays on this device). Raise the Kp level, change clouds and moonlight, wipe the clouds away with your finger, and save the sky as PNG.
wd.35: A carbon budget lab. Draw the world's CO2 emissions from today to 2100 and a simplified, published climate model turns them into CO2 levels and global warming, showing when 1.5 °C and 2 °C would be crossed.
wh.35: Drag on the emissions chart or start from a ready path, then adjust the science dials. Download the data as CSV or save the chart as PNG. It is a teaching model, not a forecast.
wd.36: Starfall Run: fly a scout ship in 3D through three sectors toward real neighbouring stars: Proxima Centauri, Barnard's Star and Sirius. Shoot or dodge asteroids, collect energy cells for your shield and dive through the jump gates. The earlier journey simulator with real distances is the second tab.
wh.36: Press Launch. Computer: steer with the mouse, click or press Space to fire, Shift to boost. Phone: drag anywhere to steer; the lasers fire on their own and Boost is on the right.
wd.37: Galaxy World. Two hundred thousand stars on real orbits in a spiral galaxy you can shape, then fly into to find our Sun.
wh.37: Drag to orbit and pinch to zoom. The buttons show the galaxy from above, edge-on, near the Sun or inside the core. In the panel, change the arm twist, bulge and bar, or pick the Milky Way, the Whirlpool or an elliptical.
wd.38: Solar System World. Every planet exactly where it is today, on real orbits, with true or readable scales and the facts of each world.
wh.38: Drag to orbit and pinch to zoom. Tap a planet to fly to it and follow it. In the panel, run time faster or jump by years, and switch between true and readable sizes and distances.
wd.39: Astronomy World. Tonight's real sky over any city, seen from an observatory: stars, constellations, the Moon and the planets in their true places.
wh.39: Drag to look around the sky and pinch or scroll to zoom. Pick a city and move the clock in the panel. Tap a star, a planet or the Moon and the telescope turns to it. The buttons look straight up, face south or look through the telescope.
wd.40: Science Discovery World. A hall of four experiments that changed what we know: measure the Earth, time Galileo's ramp, find the electron's charge and discover the atomic nucleus.
wh.40: Use the buttons to walk to each experiment, or tap one in the hall. Each has its own controls in the panel: the distance between cities, the ramp angle, the plate voltage or the alpha energy. Your results appear as you measure.
wd.41: Demolition Lab: real 3D physics. Every block has mass, friction and bounce, and wood, stone and glass behave differently. Eight challenges, a sandbox for building, and the gravity of Earth, the Moon, Mars or Jupiter. The earlier 2D playground is the second tab.
wh.41: Pick a challenge or the sandbox. Choose a tool (cannon, blast, wrecking ball or build), then click or tap the scene to use it. Drag to orbit, use the wheel or pinch to zoom. Clear every amber block with the shots you have.
wd.42: Reaction workbench. Type any chemical equation and it is balanced exactly, then every atom flies from the reactants to the products so you can see nothing is created or lost. Molar masses use standard atomic weights; enter grams to find the limiting reactant and the yield.
wh.42: Type an equation in the panel, such as C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O, and press “Balance and react” (or Enter), or pick one of the example reactions. Capital letters matter: Co is cobalt, CO is carbon monoxide. Then change the grams of each reactant to see which one runs out first and how much of each product you get.
wd.43: Heartbeat lab. A beating heart driven by a real physiology model. Change heart rate, how hard it squeezes, filling, vessel resistance and artery stiffness, and watch the pressure-volume loop, pressure traces, an ECG, blood pressure and cardiac output respond. A teaching model, not medical advice.
wh.43: Pick a situation, such as “Hard exercise” or “Heart failure”, or move the sliders yourself. The loop on the right shows one heartbeat: filling, squeezing with both valves shut, pumping out, and relaxing. Below are the pressures in the ventricle, the aorta and the atrium with an ECG. Tick “Heart sounds” to hear the valves close.
wd.44: Fusion lab. Can you build a star on Earth? Set the temperature, density and confinement time of a deuterium-tritium plasma and see the fusion power, the heating it needs, the gain Q and whether it ignites, on the Lawson chart that fusion scientists use. A simplified teaching model.
wh.44: Pick a machine such as “ITER-scale” or “Too cold”, or move the sliders. Temperature is the most important: nuclei must be fast enough to fuse. Density and confinement time decide how much heat stays in. Watch the dot on the chart: above the Q = 1 line the plasma makes more fusion power than the heating you put in, above the ignition line it keeps itself hot.
wd.45: A 3D gallery where every painting is new. Ten works, each painted on your device with a real movement's method, from Pointillism to Bengali alpona, under picture lights, with a scanned bronze sculpture at the end of the hall.
wh.45: Click a painting to step up to it, or use Previous and Next. “Paint a new one” makes another original, “Keep in my exhibition” saves it on this device, and “Download” saves a large image. “Walk the hall” lets you walk freely.
wd.46: Camera school in a real 3D street. Aperture, shutter and ISO change the picture as they would on a full-frame sensor: true depth of field, motion blur on the passing cyclist, and grain.
wh.46: Choose the light, then set aperture, shutter and ISO, or press “Meter: set the shutter for me”. Tap the picture to focus. Press “Take photo”: the shot is taken as the cyclist passes, and you can download it from the film strip.
wi.46.auto: Meter: set the shutter for me
wd.47: Ink & Light Studio. A still life is lit in real 3D with a light you move, and its shading is drawn in seven pen-and-ink techniques: tone study, hatching, cross-hatching, engraving, stippling, halftone and line. The marks cover the paper as much as the value they stand for, and the studio measures how closely. Draw over it yourself, keep pieces in your gallery and download them.
wh.47: Pick a technique, then drag on the picture or use the light sliders to move the light and watch the shading redraw. “Tone study” labels the parts of light on the sphere. Choose “Draw in ink” to draw over the scene with a pen or brush, and “Move the light” to go back. “New arrangement” sets up a fresh still life. “Save to my gallery” keeps a picture in this browser and “Download” saves a large PNG.
wd.48: Systems that draw. Five real generative algorithms grow artwork live: a particle flow field, Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion, differential growth, circle packing and a Physarum slime mould. Every work comes from a recipe of system, settings and seed, so the same recipe always grows the same piece. Touch the canvas to intervene, keep recipes in your lab book, and export PNG or plotter-ready SVG.
wh.48: Pick an algorithm and watch it grow; touch the canvas to add particles, chemicals, loops, circles or food. Change the sliders or the palette to try a variation, and press “New seed” for a different work from the same rules. “Keep this recipe” saves it to your lab book so you can grow it again. “Download PNG” saves a large image and “Download SVG” a vector file for the line and circle systems. Space pauses.
wd.49: Letter Foundry. Design a typeface of your own the way letters were made before computers, as a skeleton written with a pen. Every letter, number and mark is an original skeleton, and a monoline pen, a broad nib or a pointed pen writes it. Set weight, contrast, width, x-height, squareness, slant, spacing and serifs, type your own text, check characters per line, save your fonts and download PNG or SVG.
wh.49: Type your text in the box, pick a style under “Start from”, then change the pen and the sliders and watch every letter respond. The guide lines show the baseline, x-height, cap height, ascender and descender. “Save to my fonts” keeps the design in this browser; “Download PNG” and “Download SVG” save the setting.
wi.49.miss: This typeface covers Latin letters, numbers and basic punctuation. Not drawn yet:
wd.50: Colour Vision Lab. Colour is what three kinds of cone make of a spectrum, and everything here is computed that way, from 380 to 730 nm through the CIE 1931 observer. Overlap coloured lamps whose spectra add, mix paints the way pigments really absorb, and meet metamers: two paints that match in daylight and split under a bulb. See any of it as people with colour blindness see it.
wh.50: Choose “Lights”, “Paints” or “Metamers”. Drag the circles to overlap them; for lamps, set each one’s peak wavelength, band width and brightness, or try “Two lamps make white”. For paints, pick three pigments and a light. In Metamers press “New pair” and switch the light to watch a perfect match break; “Let my eyes adapt to the light” mimics how your eyes adjust. Choose a type of colour vision to see everything as others do.
wi.50.adapt: Let my eyes adapt to the light
wd.51: Wet Paper Studio. A watercolour sheet where paint behaves like paint: water spreads and soaks, pigment rides the flow, washes dry with a darker rim, granulating colours settle into the paper's grain, and layers glaze instead of covering. Paint wet-in-wet, drop in clean water for a bloom, lift with a tissue, tilt the board, then keep or download your paintings.
wh.51: Pick a pigment from the round swatches and paint on the sheet. “Wet brush” lays water and colour; drop another colour in while it is still wet. “Clean water” on a damp wash makes a bloom, “Dry brush” catches only the paper's grain and “Tissue lift” takes paint out. Tick “Tilt the board” to let washes run. “Dry it now” stops all movement. “Save to my paintings” keeps a picture in this browser and “Download” saves a large PNG.
wd.52: Storyboard Studio. Film grammar you can test: put real cameras on a floor plan of a room with two characters, and each frame is drawn in true perspective from its position, height and lens. The studio reads every frame like an editor, from extreme wide to extreme close-up, and warns when a cut breaks the 180-degree rule or risks a jump cut. Write action or dialogue under each frame and download the board.
wh.52: Click a frame in the strip (or use the arrow keys) to choose a shot. On the floor plan, drag a camera to move it, drag its round handle to aim it, or drag A and B. Set the camera height and lens, or use a classic set-up such as “Over A's shoulder” or “Close-up on A”. “Add shot” extends the sequence; red marks warn of a cut across the line, amber of a jump cut. “Download the board” saves every frame with its caption.
wd.53: Vibration Machines. Two old experiments where physics makes the art. On a Chladni plate, sand bounces off the parts of a vibrating plate that move and settles on the lines that stay still, drawing a different figure at every resonance; you can hear the tone as you tune it. On a harmonograph, two swinging pendulums guide a pen, and their frequency ratio, phase and friction decide the drawing. Keep the ones you like and download them as PNG or SVG.
wh.53: Choose “Chladni plate” or “Harmonograph”. On the plate, use “Next resonance ▶” (or the arrow keys, or drag sideways on the plate) and watch the sand gather; “Sound on” lets you hear the driving tone. On the harmonograph, pick a frequency ratio, adjust detuning, phase and friction, then “Draw again” or “Surprise me”. “Keep this one” saves the settings, and “Download SVG” gives a line file a pen plotter can draw.
wi.53.lines: Show where the plate stays still
wd.54: Infinite Zoom Gallery. Two pictures that never run out. In the fractal wing, a live Mandelbrot explorer computes every pixel from z → z² + c, so you can dive ten trillion times deeper and still find new shapes, fly to famous places and see the Julia set of the point you are looking at. In the second wing, a picture contains itself: paint a scene, place a frame, and the scene repeats inside it forever, turning into a spiral when the frame is tilted. Keep views, download PNG, or record the loop as a video.
wh.54: In “Fractal deep zoom”, scroll or pinch to zoom where you point, drag to move, double-click to dive, or choose a place under “Fly to”. Change “Colours” and “Colour bands”, or press “Cycle the colours”. In “Picture inside itself”, paint on the picture, switch the hand to “Move the frame” to drag it, and set “Frame size” and “Frame tilt”. “Start from” gives a scene or your own photo. “Keep this view” saves it, and “Record the loop (video)” saves one seamless loop.
wi.54.limit: This is as deep as ordinary 64-bit numbers can go (about 10¹³×). Going further needs arbitrary-precision arithmetic, which this page does not fake.
wd.55: AI Universe. A small solar system of ideas that shaped artificial intelligence, and every planet runs the real method in your browser, with no remote AI and nothing pretended. Shannon's 1948 text machine writes by counting which letter follows which. The 1958 perceptron learns a dividing line from your points and honestly fails on XOR. A* search, made for the Shakey robot, finds the shortest way through a maze you draw. Minimax, the idea behind Deep Blue, plays noughts and crosses and shows you how it scores each move.
wh.55: Click a planet on the map, or choose one under “Planet”. On the text machine, change “Memory” and “Temperature”, then “Write again”, or paste your own text. On the perceptron, click to add points, then “Start learning”, and try “XOR (no line works)”. On A* search, draw walls, move the start and goal, and compare the methods. In the game, click a square (or press 1 to 9) and use “Look-ahead” to make the machine weaker or perfect.
wi.55.g.draw: A draw. With perfect play on both sides, this game always ends in a draw.
wd.56: A six-axis industrial robot arm in a factory cell, with real inverse kinematics, straight-line moves, a conveyor and a teach pendant, plus a PID line-following robot.
wh.56: Tap a crate, then tap where it should go. Teach your own program in Program, turn each joint in Joints, and tune the line robot in Line robot.
wi.56.w.reach: Out of reach: the arm stretches toward it
wd.57: A quantum computer hanging in a gold dilution refrigerator. Build circuits on up to five qubits and watch exact amplitudes, Bloch spheres and 1,000 real measurements.
wh.57: Pick a gate and tap the circuit grid, or start from an example. Press Play in Measure to step through it, and use Views to fly around the chamber.
wd.58: Page-Load Simulator. What happens between pressing Enter and seeing a web page, computed millisecond by millisecond: DNS lookups, TCP and TLS handshakes, TCP slow start, the six-connection limit of HTTP/1.1 and multiplexing in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, render-blocking CSS and scripts, late fonts and lazy photos. Change the network and the techniques, watch the waterfall and the paint and load times move, and keep runs side by side. A teaching model, not a measurement of any real site.
wh.58: Pick a network preset (“Slow mobile”, “4G”, “Fibre”, “Satellite”) or set the round-trip time and bandwidth. Switch between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, change the number of photos, and turn the techniques on and off. Each bar shows a file's waiting, handshakes and download; the dashed lines mark the first paint (FCP), the largest paint (LCP) and the full load. “Keep this run” adds it to the comparison table.
wi.58.defer: Defer scripts (do not block the first paint)
wd.59: Turtle Studio. Write small programs that draw, in a friendly Logo language built for this world. Move the turtle, change colour and width, loop with repeat, make your own commands with inputs, and use if, stop and random to grow spirals, flowers, recursive trees and snowflakes. The language has its own interpreter, so nothing you type runs as JavaScript; errors point to the line, endless loops are stopped safely, and you can keep sketches and download PNG or SVG.
wh.59: Type a program in the box and press “Run ▶” (or Ctrl+Enter), or pick one under “Examples”. Commands: fd and bk move, rt and lt turn, pu and pd lift and lower the pen, color, hue and width style the line, repeat n [ … ] loops, “to name :input … end” defines a command, and if … [stop] ends recursion. Open “Language reference” for the full list. “Keep this sketch” saves it; download PNG or SVG.
wd.60: Machine Learning Explorer. Watch a real neural network learn in your browser. In the boundary lab it learns to separate coloured points (a ring, four corners, two spirals or your own clicks), with the decision region, the network’s weights and the loss curve updating live, and a held-out test set that shows when it memorises instead of learning. In the doodle trainer you name three things, draw a few examples of each, train a small network on them, and watch it guess your new drawings. Everything is computed on your device; nothing is sent anywhere.
wh.60: Boundary lab: pick a data set, press “Train” and watch the shaded region change. Try fewer neurons or one layer on the spirals to see it fail, or tick “Also give it x², y² and x·y” to make a ring easy. With “My own points”, click to add gold or blue points. Doodle trainer: rename the three things, draw on the pad and press “+ name” to add each example (five each works well), then “Train on my examples” and draw something new.
wi.60.sq: Also give it x², y² and x·y
wi.60.name: Name
wi.60.empty: Draw something on the pad first.
wi.60.few: Add at least one example of each thing first.
wi.60.untrained: Not trained yet: add examples, then train.
wi.60.trained: Trained. Draw something new and watch the guess.
wi.60.cv: A neural network learning: coloured regions show what it predicts, or a drawing pad where it guesses your doodles.
wi.60.a.b: Each point is gold or blue. The network sees only its x and y, guesses a colour, and nudges its weights to be less wrong (backpropagation). The shaded background is its guess for every spot. 30% of the points are kept aside as a test: if training accuracy is high but test accuracy is low, it has memorised instead of learned.
wi.60.a.d: Choose three things to teach, draw a few examples of each on the pad, then train. The network (256 inputs, 32 hidden neurons, 3 outputs) learns only from your drawings, shifted a little to make more examples. With five or more examples each it usually tells them apart; with one it mostly guesses.
wd.61: Interactive Data World. A small data studio in your browser. Explore Anscombe’s famous quartet (four data sets with the same statistics and very different pictures), live dice rolls that grow into a bell curve, the real load timings of this page measured by your own browser, points you click, or your own CSV file, which never leaves your device. Columns are typed and summarised automatically; draw a scatter plot with a fitted line and correlation, a histogram, bars or a line, split into panels by a category, drag points to see how one value moves the result, and save the chart or the table.
wh.61: Pick a data set under “Data”, then a chart. For Anscombe’s quartet, compare the four panels and their identical r, then drag a point. For dice, raise “Dice per roll” and watch the bell curve appear. For your own data choose “My own CSV”, paste a table with a header row and press “Use this table”. Hover any mark to read its values; the table under the chart summarises every numeric column. Save the chart as PNG or the table as CSV.
wi.61.a.ans: Four small data sets published by the statistician Francis Anscombe in 1973. All four have almost the same mean, spread, correlation (0.816) and fitted line, yet the pictures are completely different. Drag any point to see how one value moves the line.
wi.61.a.dice: Real random rolls made in your browser just now (not real-world data). Watch the histogram of the sum: with more dice it turns into a bell curve.
wi.61.a.page: Measured by your own browser: every file this page loaded, with its type, start time, duration and size. Numbers differ on each device and visit; cached files show 0 kB transferred.
wi.61.a.clicks: Click the chart to add points in the chosen group, drag to move them, and right-click a point to delete it (on a touch screen, use Clear points). They are kept in this browser only.
wi.61.a.csv: Paste a table with a header row, or open a .csv file. It is read in your browser and kept only here; nothing is uploaded. Up to 5,000 rows.
wi.61.big: That file is larger than 2 MB; please use a smaller one.
wi.61.cv: A chart of the chosen data: scatter plot, histogram, bars or line, optionally split into panels.
wi.61.emptyc: Click anywhere here to add points.
wd.62: Blockchain Learning Space. See how a blockchain really works, with real SHA-256 hashing written for this world and checked against the official test vectors. Fingerprint text or a file and watch about half the bits flip when one letter changes; build a chain of blocks, mine them by searching for a nonce, and see one edit break every block after it; then run three peers, try to cheat on one, and learn why the chain with the most work wins. No coins, wallets or network: everything happens in this page.
wh.62: Start in “Hash lab”: type anything and press “Change one letter” to see the avalanche of flipped bits, or fingerprint a file. In “Chain”, edit a block’s data and watch it and the blocks after it turn red, then press “Mine” or “Re-mine everything broken”; raise the difficulty to feel each extra zero cost about 16 times more work. In “Peers”, follow steps 1 to 4 in order.
wi.62.honest: This is a teaching model in your browser: no coins, wallets or network. Real blockchains add digital signatures, transaction rules and thousands of computers, but the hashing and linking shown here work the same way.
wi.62.a.hash: A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of any data. The same input always gives the same 64 characters, a tiny change gives a completely different one, and there is no practical way to go backwards from the fingerprint to the data.
wi.62.cmp: Highlighted: what changed compared with the previous version. On average about 128 of the 256 bits flip, whatever you change.
wi.62.big: Please choose a file under 50 MB.
wi.62.filehint: compare this with the SHA-256 a download page publishes to check the file is untouched.
wi.62.filenote: Files are read only inside this page and never uploaded.
wi.62.a.chain: Each block stores its data, the hash of the block before it and a number called the nonce. Mining tries nonce after nonce until the block’s hash starts with enough zeros. Change the data in any block: its hash changes, so it and every block after it break. Fixing them means mining them all again.
wi.62.diffnote: The rule changed: blocks mined for the old difficulty may now be broken. Each extra zero needs about 16 times more tries.
wi.62.disagrees: Its copy differs from the others.
wi.62.a.peers: Three computers keep their own copy of the same chain. Try to cheat on peer B: change an old payment, then re-mine B so its chain is valid again. The other two still hold the original, so B is outnumbered. Real networks follow the valid chain with the most mining work, so B only wins if it can out-mine everyone else together.
wi.62.n1: Block 1 changed: its hash no longer meets the rule and every later block points to a hash that is gone.
wi.62.n2b: B has nothing broken to re-mine.
wi.62.n2: B is valid again, but its tip differs from A and C and its chain is not longer than theirs, so they keep their own.
wi.62.n3: B now has the most work. If A and C follow the rule, they switch to B’s version, cheat included. This is why an attacker needs more mining power than everyone else.
wi.62.switched: Switched to the chain of peer
wi.62.kept: Kept its own chain: no valid chain has more work.
wd.63: Fly inside a real chip: a 4-bit adder built from gates you can switch, an 8-bit computer whose 512 memory bits are LEDs on the die, and tools for error correction and compression.
wh.63: Flip the switches in Adder, write and run assembly in Computer, and try error correction and compression in Codes.
wi.63.a.bits: Everything digital is stored as bits: switches that are 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte, which can mean a number from 0 to 255, a signed number from -128 to 127, or a letter. The ASCII table, published in 1963, says which number is which letter: 65 is A.
wi.63.type: Type a letter to see its bits
wi.63.a.adder: A computer adds with logic gates. One full adder takes two bits and a carry and uses two XOR gates, two AND gates and one OR gate to make a sum bit and a carry out. Chain four of them and you can add numbers up to 15 + 15. Flip the input bits and follow the signals.
wi.63.gates: Four full adders: each passes its carry to the left
wi.63.a.cpu: A complete computer in miniature: 64 bytes of memory that hold both the program and its data, one register (A), a program counter (PC) and a few instructions. Every real processor runs the same loop billions of times a second: fetch an instruction, do it, move on.
wi.63.refs: LDA x: copy memory x into A · STA x: copy A into memory x · ADD x / SUB x: add or subtract memory x (wraps at 256 and sets the carry) · LDI n: put the number n in A · JMP x: jump to x · JZ x: jump if A is 0 · JC x: jump if the last ADD/SUB carried · OUT: print A · HLT: stop · name: DATA n reserves a byte.
wi.63.long: Stopped after 5,000 steps: the program may loop forever.
wi.63.a.ham: Signals get damaged on the way: a scratch on a disc, static on a radio link. Richard Hamming’s 1950 code adds three check bits to every four data bits, arranged so that any single flipped bit can be found and fixed. Set the data, then flip one bit of the message in transit.
wi.63.sent: Sent: seven bits (p1, p2 and p3 are check bits)
wi.63.transit: Received: click a bit to damage it on the way
wi.63.clean: All three checks pass: no error.
wi.63.ham2: With two flipped bits this code is fooled and “fixes” the wrong one; stronger codes in phones, QR codes and space probes handle many errors at once.
wi.63.htext: she sells sea shells by the sea shore
wi.63.a.huff: Compression saves space by giving common symbols short codes and rare ones long codes. David Huffman’s 1952 method builds the best such code for your text by repeatedly joining the two rarest symbols. No code is the start of another, so the bits can be read back without separators.
wi.63.rt: Decoded back from the bits: identical to your text.
wi.63.huff2: The code table must also be stored or agreed in advance, so very short texts can end up larger in practice. Try a long text with few different letters, then one with many.
wd.64: Future Interfaces. An input lab where you try two real research tools that people use to invent and judge new ways of controlling computers. Draw single-stroke gestures that turn into clean shapes with the $1 Unistroke Recognizer, and teach it gestures of your own. Then take a Fitts's law pointing test that measures your own speed in bits per second, so you can compare mouse, touch and pen.
wh.64: Choose an experiment. In “Gesture commands”, draw one stroke on the canvas: a circle, triangle, rectangle or star becomes a shape, a check mark fills the last shape, and a scribble deletes one. To add your own gesture, draw it, type a name and press “Teach the last stroke as this gesture”. In “Pointing test”, press “Start the test”, then tap the ring and the target, 18 times.
wi.64.cv: An input lab: draw gestures that become shapes, or hit targets to measure your pointing speed.
wi.64.short: Too short: draw a bigger gesture.
wi.64.unsure2: Try again, or teach it as a new gesture.
wi.64.fill: Check mark: filled the last shape.
wi.64.nothing2: Check mark: draw a shape first.
wi.64.teach0: Draw the gesture first, then teach it.
wi.64.teachq: Type a name for the gesture first (for example: heart, arrow, spiral).
wi.64.taught2: Draw it again and it will be recognised.
wi.64.a.g: Draw one stroke on the canvas. A circle, triangle, rectangle or star becomes a clean shape where you drew it. A check mark fills the last shape. A scribble over a shape deletes it. The recogniser compares your stroke with stored examples after resampling it to 64 points and turning, scaling and centring it, so size, position and drawing speed do not matter.
wi.64.teach: Teach the last stroke as this gesture
wi.64.a.f: Every new input device, from the mouse to touch screens and eye tracking, is compared with a Fitts's law test. Tap the ring in the middle, then the target as fast as you can while staying accurate. 18 trials mix three distances and three sizes. The world fits time = a + b × difficulty, where difficulty = log2(distance / width + 1) bits, and reports your throughput.
wi.64.hint: Draw a circle, triangle, rectangle or star here
wi.64.again: Try again with another device to compare.
wd.65: World Explorer. A live map of the real Earth that you can turn into a spinning globe, the Mercator map or the Equal Earth map. It shows day and night for this very minute (or any date and hour), the shortest route between two cities with distance, heading, a rough flight time and each city's local clock and day length, and identical 600 km circles that reveal how each map stretches the planet. Everything is computed in your browser.
wh.65: Drag the map to turn it. Choose a view: Globe, Mercator or Equal Earth. Pick two cities in “From” and “To”, or click city dots on the map. Untick “Live” and move the date and hour sliders to see the seasons and the midnight sun. Tick the circles to compare how much each map distorts. Click anywhere else to read its position and the Sun's height there.
wi.65.cv: A map of the Earth with day and night, city routes and distortion circles. Drag to turn it; click a city to choose it.
wi.65.a.globe: The globe is the only view without distortion, but you can see just half the world at once. Drag to spin it.
wi.65.a.merc: Mercator (1569) keeps compass directions true, which made it the sailors' map, but it blows up areas towards the poles: Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is in fact about 14 times larger. Turn on the circles to see it.
wi.65.a.ee: Equal Earth (2018) keeps every area in its true proportion, so Africa looks as big as it really is, at the cost of some bending of shapes near the edges.
wi.65.foot: Coastlines: Natural Earth 1:110m (public domain). Flight time is distance ÷ 850 km/h + 30 minutes, a rough guide only; real routes follow winds and airways.
wd.66: Global Architecture. Two drawing rooms about forms that travelled between cultures. In the star-pattern studio, geometric star patterns of the kind seen on mosques, madrasas and palaces from Spain to Bengal grow from a plain tiling by Hankin's “polygons in contact” method; change the tiling, angle and colours and download the result as SVG. In Arches of the world, the same opening is spanned by round, segmental, pointed, horseshoe, four-centred, ogee and catenary arches built from stones you can count.
wh.66: Choose a room. In “Star patterns”, pick a starting tiling and move “Contact angle” to grow stars; “Line split” doubles each line, and “Download SVG” saves a vector file. In “Arches of the world”, choose an arch, change its shape and the number of stones, and compare the rise for the same 4 m opening.
wi.66.cv: A drawing of a geometric star pattern or of an arch made of stones.
wi.66.ad.round: Rise is exactly half the span. Used by Roman builders in aqueducts and bridges, and later in Romanesque churches.
wi.66.ad.segmental: A slice of a circle, flatter than a half circle, so it pushes harder sideways and needs strong abutments. Common over windows and in bridges.
wi.66.ad.pointed: Two arcs meeting at a point. Used across the Islamic world and later in Gothic cathedrals; the point lets the rise change without changing the span.
wi.66.ad.horseshoe: The curve continues below the widest point. Typical of Moorish Spain and North Africa, as in the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
wi.66.ad.fourc: Small arcs at the sides and large flat arcs to the top. Seen in Persian and Mughal iwans and gateways, and in English Tudor doorways.
wi.66.ad.ogee: Each side is an S curve, convex below and concave above. Decorative rather than strong; found in Venetian Gothic and in many South Asian buildings.
wi.66.ad.catenary: The shape of a hanging chain turned upside down, which carries its own weight in pure compression (Robert Hooke, 1675). Used by Antoni Gaudí.
wi.66.ab.star: Many star patterns on historic buildings can be drawn from a plain tiling. From the middle of each edge send two lines into the tile at the same angle, and stop each line where it meets its neighbour. E. H. Hankin described this in 1925. Small angles give a lattice; bigger angles grow stars and rosettes.
wi.66.ab.arch: The same opening, spanned seven ways. Every arch is a ring of wedge-shaped stones (voussoirs) that press on each other; the shape decides how high it rises, how hard it pushes sideways, and how it looks.
wi.66.key: the darker middle stone is the keystone
wd.67: Cultural Discovery. How cultures count days and write numbers, computed live. See one date in eleven calendars at once, from the revised Bengali calendar of Bangladesh to the Islamic, Hebrew, Chinese, Persian, Indian, Ethiopian and Japanese calendars, with rings that show how far through its year each one is and when its next new year comes. Then write any number in Bengali, Devanagari, Arabic, Thai, Tibetan and other digits, in Chinese characters and Roman numerals, and as Maya dots and bars and Babylonian wedges.
wh.67: Choose a room. In “Calendars”, pick a date or press “Today”, “Pohela Boishakh” or “21 February”, and use −1 and +1 to step one day. In “Numbers”, type any whole number up to 99,999,999 or press one of the examples.
wi.67.ab.cal: The same day has many names. Some calendars follow the Sun, some the Moon, some both; their years start on different days. Each ring shows how far through its own year this date is. The Bengali calendar follows the revised Bangladesh rules; the others come from your browser's calendar engine. Any of them can differ by a day from official announcements or local moon sighting.
wi.67.ab.num: Digits look different around the world, but most modern systems, including Bengali and Devanagari, work like the Western ones: ten symbols and place value, an idea that came from India. Chinese characters name the powers of ten instead. The Maya counted in twenties with dots and bars and had a zero; the Babylonians counted in sixties with two wedge signs, which is why an hour has 60 minutes.
wi.67.rings: Rings: how far through its year each calendar is on this date
wi.67.toobig: Romans had no standard way past 3,999
wd.68: Travel Photography. A field kit that works offline. The light planner shows, for 40 cities and any date, sunrise, sunset, the golden and blue hours in the city's own time and the direction the light comes from, worked out from the Sun's position in your browser. The composition desk lets you frame your own photo, which never leaves your device, with thirds, golden-ratio, spiral and diagonal guides, crop ratios, straightening, a live histogram and full-size export.

wi.28.title: Ocean World
wi.28.sub: A living sea built from real wave physics. Sail the swell, then dive to the reef.
wi.28.p.waves: Every wave here obeys ω² = g·k·tanh(k·h). Longer periods make longer, faster waves; shallow water slows them down.
wi.28.p.dive: Water swallows red light first, then orange and green. Only blue reaches the deep.
wi.28.k.buoyt: Waves move energy, not water. The buoy only circles: forward on the crest, back in the trough. The bright loop is its path over one wave period.
wi.29.title: Forest World
wi.29.sub: One hectare of woodland grows tree by tree. Pioneers race for the light, patient species take over, and every fire or storm starts the story again.
wi.29.chart: Trees of each species over time
wi.29.how: Each year every tree grows by how much light reaches its crown past taller neighbours. Birch needs full sun; beech can wait in the shade for a century, then take over. Under a closed canopy the grass dies back to leaf litter. This is ecological succession.
wi.29.honest: A simplified model for learning. Carbon uses the Chave et al. (2014) allometric equation with estimated trunk diameters.

wi.30.title: Wildlife Kingdom
wi.30.sub: A meadow at golden hour. Every hare and fox lives, eats and breeds by itself, and the populations rise and fall in cycles.
wi.30.nofox: The fox model could not load; the meadow still runs
wi.30.chart: Population chart: hares and foxes over time, with the Lotka–Volterra model dashed
wi.30.how: Hares gain energy from grass and foxes from hares; both spend it moving. With food to spare they breed. More hares feed more foxes, the foxes eat the hares down and then starve, and the hares recover. Grazed patches turn short and dry, then grow back.
wi.30.lv: The dashed lines are the Lotka–Volterra equations, dH/dt = aH − bHF and dF/dt = dHF − cF. The living meadow adds grass, space and chance, so its cycles are messier, like real ones.

wi.37.title: Galaxy World
wi.37.sub: Two hundred thousand stars on real orbits. Shape the arms, then fly in to find our Sun.
wi.37.p.phys: Spiral arms are traffic jams of stars, not fixed chains of stars. Try material arms to see why: the inside turns faster, so the arms wind up within a few turns.
wi.37.k.sunt: About 26,000 light-years from the centre, between two arms. The Sun takes about 230 million years to go round once: the last time it was here, the first dinosaurs were appearing.

wi.38.p.time: Positions use JPL's orbital elements for this exact date. Speed time up to watch Mercury lap the Sun four times while Earth goes round once.
wi.38.p.scale: Space is mostly empty. At true size the planets are specks: Earth is 23,000 of its own widths from the Sun.

wi.40.title: Science Discovery World
wi.40.sub: Four experiments that changed what we know. Run them yourself and find the answer in your own data.
wi.40.m.move: Not still yet: change the voltage until the drop hangs in the air
wi.40.e.h: Eratosthenes · the size of the Earth
wi.40.e.p: At noon on midsummer the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene, but in Alexandria a stick cast a shadow. The shadow angle is the slice of the whole circle between the two cities.
wi.40.g.p: The bells sit at distances 1, 4, 9 and 16. If distance grows with time squared, the ball rings them on an even beat.
wi.40.m.h: Millikan · the charge of the electron
wi.40.m.p: Tiny oil drops pick up a few extra electrons. Turn the voltage until the ringed drop hangs still: the electric pull then equals its weight, and that gives its charge.
wi.40.r.h: Rutherford · the atom is mostly empty
wi.40.r.p: If atoms were soft puddings of charge, every alpha particle would pass straight through. Watch for the rare ones that bounce back: they hit a tiny, heavy nucleus.
wi.113.title: Rain World
wi.113.sub: A city street in the rain. Change the weather and the hour, then stand under an awning and listen.
wi.113.honest: Everything here is drawn live by your graphics chip: falling rain at real drop speeds, splashes, ripples, reflections in the wet road and thunder that arrives late, as it does, because sound travels about 343 m each second. The water is a visual effect, not a fluid simulation. Phones get fewer drops and simpler reflections to stay cool.
